AbstractThis is a pilot study developing a sound system for 
the esophageal stethoscope to continuously monitor the patient 
condition during surgery. The microphone base sound recording 
system was composed of an esophageal stethoscope coupler and a 
preamplifier, and it was confirmed that it is possible to monitor 
heart sound and respiration during anesthesia. 
. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
The heart and breath sounds measured by the esophageal 
stethoscope include important information about myocardial 
contractility and blood vessel status, which is an important 
factor for the anesthesiologi st to diagnose the patient's 
condition during surgery and operation. These heart sounds 
are also useful for the diagnosis of arrhythmia or myocardial 
ischemia, and in particular, ra pid detection of changes in 
hemodynamics is very important in preventing heart failure 
[1-2]. 
In this paper, we conducted a pilot study to develop 
esophageal stethoscope sound recording system by condenser 
microphone for monitor the status of the patient during 
anesthesia.
II. METHODS 
The developed esophageal stethoscope auditory system is 
shown in Fig. 1. It consists of a coupler that take into account 
the acoustical aspects and a microphone preamplifier. The 
coupler was designed to minimize the noise coming from the 
outside of the operating room by putting a cavity for sound 
insulation on the outer wall and using ABS material using 3D 
printer (B210S, Korbot co.). 
The heart sound delivered through the esophageal 
stethoscope was amplified through a electret condenser 
microphone (POM-3535P-R, PUI Audio co.) and a 
preamplifier. The gain of the preamplifier was 68 dB. In 
addition, the power source has secured the safety of the patient 
by using a power source complying with the international 
standard, IEC60601-1, for electrical and mechanical safety for 
electronic medical devices.

The developed esophageal stethoscope auditory system is 
shown in Fig. 1. It consists of a coupler that take into account

outside of the operating room by putting a cavity for sound

by using a power source complying with the international 
standard, IEC60601-1, for electrical and mechanical safety for 
electronic medical devices. 
 
*This research was supported by the Bio & Medical Technology 
Development Program of the NRF funded by the Korean government, MSIP 
(NRF-2016M3A9F1941328). 
S. Jung, Y. Kang, D.Y. Lee and Y. Yun are with the Department of 
Convergence Biomedical Engineering, Daelim University, Anyang, South 
Korea. (corresponding authors to provide phone: +82-31-467-4433; fax: 
+82-31-467-4432; e-mail: yhyun@daelim.ac.kr). 
H. Shin is with the Dept. of Biomedical Engineering, Chonnam National 
University, Yeosu, South Korea (phone: +82-61-659-7362; fax: +82-61-659- 
7369; e-mail: hangsik.shin@jnu.ac.kr). 
Amplified heart sounds were recorded at a sampling 
frequency of 1 kHz using a 16-bit ADC (Powerlab 16/35, 
ADInstruments co.). 
III. RESULTS 
Using the proposed system, it was confirmed that heart 
sound was recorded well for anesthetized patients. We will 
improve the acoustical characteris tics of the coupler part in 
the future, minimize the noise caused by the pressure change 
of the low frequency band, and improve the measurement 
reliability of the heart sound me asurement by developing a 
calibration device for quantitative measurement.
